briefs.sun: The Sun is our star — a huge ball of hot plasma that holds the Solar System together. Never look at it directly or through optics without a proper solar filter.
briefs.moon: Earth's only natural satellite. The same side always faces us, and its phases come from how much of the sunlit half we see.
briefs.mercury: The smallest planet and the closest to the Sun. It never strays far from the Sun, so look for it low in twilight.
briefs.venus: The brightest planet, wrapped in thick clouds of carbon dioxide. Often called the Morning or Evening Star.
briefs.mars: The Red Planet. Its colour comes from iron oxide dust; it has the tallest volcano in the Solar System, Olympus Mons.
briefs.jupiter: The largest planet, a gas giant with the Great Red Spot. Binoculars show its four large Galilean moons.
briefs.saturn: The ringed planet. Even a small telescope reveals its rings, made of countless pieces of ice and rock.
briefs.uranus: An ice giant tilted on its side. At the limit of naked-eye visibility under very dark skies.
briefs.neptune: The most distant planet, an ice giant with the fastest winds in the Solar System. A telescope is needed to see it.
briefs.M1: The remnant of a supernova seen from Earth in 1054. At its centre spins a pulsar.
briefs.M8: A large star-forming cloud in Sagittarius, visible to the naked eye under dark skies.
briefs.M13: One of the finest globular clusters of the northern sky: several hundred thousand stars packed into a ball.
briefs.M27: One of the brightest planetary nebulae — the glowing shell thrown off by a dying star.
briefs.M31: The Andromeda Galaxy, the nearest large galaxy to the Milky Way and the most distant object easily visible to the naked eye.
briefs.M42: The Orion Nebula, a stellar nursery visible to the naked eye in Orion's sword.
briefs.M44: The Beehive Cluster in Cancer, a beautiful sight in binoculars.
briefs.M45: The Pleiades, or Seven Sisters — a young, bright cluster of hot blue stars.
briefs.M51: The Whirlpool Galaxy, a classic face-on spiral interacting with a smaller companion.
briefs.M57: The Ring Nebula in Lyra, a small smoke-ring-like planetary nebula.
briefs.M104: The Sombrero Galaxy, seen almost edge-on with a prominent dark dust lane.

meteors.title: Meteor showers
meteors.zhrExplain: ZHR (Zenithal Hourly Rate) is how many meteors one ideal observer would see in an hour with the radiant straight overhead, a perfectly dark sky (stars down to magnitude 6.5) and nothing blocking the view. It is not a promise: real counts are usually much lower.
meteors.radiantHint: You don't need to stare at the radiant: meteors appear all over the sky, their trails only seem to spread out from it. Looking 30–50° away from it shows longer trails.
meteors.whatIsRadiant: The radiant is the point from which meteor trails appear to spread out. Meteors of one shower fly on parallel paths; perspective makes them seem to come from one spot, like railway tracks meeting in the distance.
meteors.approxDates: Typical dates — verified data for this year are not bundled yet.
meteors.estimateNote: This is an estimate of observing conditions, not a prediction of how many meteors you will see.
meteors.source: Shower data: IMO Meteor Shower Calendar 2026.

desc.qua: A short, sharp shower at the start of January: the maximum lasts only a few hours. Best seen from the Northern Hemisphere before dawn.
desc.lyr: One of the oldest recorded showers, active in late April. Moderate rates with occasional surprises; the radiant near Vega climbs high after midnight.
desc.eta: Dust from Halley's Comet, active from late April into May. Fast meteors, best before dawn, especially from the tropics and the Southern Hemisphere.
desc.sda: A steady shower in late July with a low southern radiant in Aquarius; best from southern latitudes and the tropics after midnight.
desc.per: The most popular shower of the year: warm August nights, fast and often bright meteors. From mid-northern latitudes the radiant is up all night and climbs higher towards dawn.
desc.dra: An early-October shower from Comet Giacobini–Zinner. Usually very weak, but it has produced rare outbursts. Unusually, its radiant is highest in the evening.
desc.ori: The second shower from Halley's Comet. Fast meteors in October; the radiant near Orion is well placed after midnight.
desc.leo: Famous for historic meteor storms; in ordinary years a modest mid-November shower of very fast meteors. The radiant in Leo rises around midnight.
desc.gem: The richest regular shower of the year, in mid-December. Slower, often bright meteors; the radiant near Castor is up most of the night, so you can start in the evening.
desc.urs: A modest shower around the December solstice, best from the Northern Hemisphere. Its radiant near the Little Dipper never sets for most northern observers.
